## DO and DON'T with AI

- **Break up** complex, vague tasks (big black boxes) into smaller steps that can be intersubjectively verified (tiny black boxes).
- **Document** your methodology so you can explain step by step, verifiably, how you reached your conclusions.
- **Use AI** to speed up many simple tasks which you *could* have done yourself if you had the time.
- **Break up the data** into pieces for AI analysis. Ideally run each piece as a separate prompt. Failing that, number each section and ask for a numbered, section-by-section answer, for example in a table.

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-warning}
## DON'T
- Give an AI large pieces of text and expect it to pay due attention to all of it. It *claims* to and may cite passages, but attention is expensive and it tries to reduce that expense. It will skim and jump to conclusions.
- Ask an AI to do maths for you, like adding up positive or negative findings on a rubric. AIs are still terrible at maths.
- Ask an AI to do *implicit* counting and comparison like "are there more positive or negative mentions of X in this report?"
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.callout-tip}
## DO
- Use explicit, manual methods (Excel?) to synthesise the results of the multiple separate tasks you gave the AI.
:::
:::

:::

# AI-led interviews??

## DO: When to use AI interviewing

- Situations where you **don't know exactly what to ask**
- Less structured, **explorative conversations**
- When your respondents may use **different languages**
- When you can **scale up** from H2H to AI interviewing

## DON'T: When not to use AI interviewing

- When you **could have used a questionnaire**
- When you have **a lot of specific questions** to ask
- When you are dealing with **sensitive information** or with **vulnerable populations**
- When you really need the **human-to-human** interaction

## Where AI interviewing fits

| Method | Quality | Quantity |
|--------|---------|----------|
| Face-to-face interviews | High | Low |
| Conversational AI interviewing | Medium-high | Medium-high |
| Structured questionnaires | Low | High |

[Bigger because so many possibilities.]{.notes}

# A case study

## A real-world case study using Qualia

**Background**

DuocUC, a higher education institution in Chile, hired our consultancy (Causal Map Ltd) to conduct QuIP-style interviews with Qualia and analyse them using the Causal Map app. The interviews were motivated by concerns about the **gender gaps faced by women pursuing STEM careers** at the university.

## Step 1: Setting up the interview in Qualia

- The instruction for the AI interviewer was similar to the **instructions you could give to a human interviewer**.
- Both the interview instructions and the interviews themselves were conducted in **Spanish**.
- The AI asked questions about changes in **3 domains**: educational experiences, professional development and relationship dynamics.
- We used GPT-4o, which was the best AI model to date.

## Step 2: Collecting stories with Qualia

- We sent the interview link to 50 people and were able to collect 32 interviews.
- We created individual links so we could track the interviews.
- We downloaded the interview results from Qualia and uploaded them into Causal Map.

## Step 3: Analysing stories with Causal Map

- We used AI (GPT-4o) to identify **each and every causal link** in the interviews, and for each link, label the cause and effect.
- We used a **"radical zero-shot" approach** in which the AI is given no codebook and is told to invent its own codes (in Spanish). We gave the AI context about the project.
- We found **251 causal links** mentioned by the respondents.
